title: A CFD geometry drawing is a contract: every labelled edge becomes a boundary condition
summary: Before a reacting-flow case can run, the domain has to be drawn, dimensioned and every edge named as an inlet, a wall or the reactor. Read these drawings as the list of what the solver will be told, and as a hint of where the flow will do something interesting: the sudden step where a narrow lance section opens into a wide reactor.

media.alt: Dimensioned 2D axisymmetric drawing of a lance and reactor. A thin inlet section 163 mm long opens at a step into a wide reactor 332 mm long, 104.5 mm tall. Numbers mark 1 air inlet, 2 lance wall, 3 coal inlet and 4 reactor; small labels give 15 mm, 9 mm and 2 mm near the lance.

source.caption: Base-case 15mm axisymmetric geometry
group: 02_slide_8-08_crop: 25mm lance variant of the same geometry
source.note: Group explainer for the four geometry drawings of the pulverised-coal-injection (PCI) tuyere study. The representative figure is the base case. Dimensions are read from the drawings; where a number is derived (a sum or a ratio) it is computed from those read-off values.

read_the_figure.question: What exactly is being simulated: which edges are inlets, which are walls, how big is each region, and where does the flow have to change shape?
read_the_figure.axes: There are no data axes. It is a to-scale engineering drawing in millimetres. In the 2D drawings the horizontal direction is the flow direction (axial) and the horizontal line at the bottom (the small x-y triad sits on it) is the axis of symmetry, so the vertical direction is radius. The 3D drawing (figure 06) is a perspective CAD view.
look_at: The yellow numbered tags and the key at lower right: here 1 air inlet, 2 lance wall, 3 coal inlet, 4 reactor. Each tag will become one boundary-condition entry in the solver.

The dimension lines: 163 mm for the narrow inlet section, 332 mm for the wide reactor, 104.5 mm for the reactor height measured from the axis. Small leader labels near the lance (15 mm, 9 mm, 2 mm) size the lance and its inlet slots.
The step at x = 163 mm where the narrow section opens into the reactor. This is a sudden expansion and the flow will separate and recirculate behind it.

The other drawings in the group: the 25 mm lance variant keeps 163 mm and 332 mm and gives a 79.5 mm step; the co-injection drawing adds a separate hydrogen inlet (tag 3) between two lance walls (tags 2 and 4) next to the coal inlet (tag 5); the 3D drawing shows a 60 mm pipe with a bend, a 1015 mm run and a honeycomb detail.
read_the_figure.proves: Nothing about the physics. The drawing proves only that the case is fully specified: each region has a size and each edge has a role. A reader can check that the sizes are consistent between variants and that nothing needed (for example a fuel inlet) is missing.
if_wrong: An unlabelled edge: the solver would apply a default wall, which silently closes an inlet or outlet.
A dimension that disagrees between variants without being flagged: results from the two cases would not be comparable.
A 2D axisymmetric picture used for a flow that is not axisymmetric (the bend and honeycomb in the real rig are not): the drawing is then a simplification, and the report should say so.
must_check: Every boundary has a label and the key lists them all.
Units and the symmetry axis are stated; in an axisymmetric drawing the axis must be the lower edge.
Whether a dimension is a radius or a diameter. In this group the leader labels mix both and the drawing does not say which is which.
Outlet location and type (pressure outlet, for example): the key does not list an outlet, so the right-hand edge is assumed.
Same dimensions across variants except the one being studied.
as_drawn: Reactor height 104.5 mm and step height 79.5 mm (25 mm variant) add to 79.5 + 25 = 104.5, so the reactor is the same in both variants and only the lance section changes. For the 15 mm base case the step height is then 104.5 - 15 = 89.5 mm (derived, not printed).
Reactor length over step height is 332 / 79.5 = 4.2 for the 25 mm variant and 332 / 89.5 = 3.7 for the base case.
Honeycomb (figure 06, printed values): outer diameter 60 mm, inner diameter 10 mm, cell size 5 mm, spacing between hexagons 0.25 mm.

terms.meaning: A 3D flow with no variation around the axis is solved on one half-plane: axial position x and radius r. The solver weights each cell by 2 pi r, so it is not the same as a flat 2D channel.
What the solver is told on an edge: inlet (flow rate, temperature, composition), wall (no slip, temperature or heat flux), outlet (pressure), axis (symmetry).
A narrow tube that injects fuel (here pulverised coal, and in the co-injection case hydrogen) into the main air stream.
The nozzle through which hot air blast and injected fuel enter a blast furnace. The drawings represent a lab-scale model of it, not the furnace.
A step in cross-section where flow separates from the wall, forms a recirculation zone and reattaches some distance downstream.
The size of the radial jump at the expansion. Reattachment length is measured in step heights.
A block of many parallel small channels. It removes swirl and evens out the velocity profile before the combustor.
The effective diameter of a non-circular channel, four times the flow area over the wetted perimeter.

remember: A geometry drawing is a specification: each numbered edge becomes a boundary condition.
In an axisymmetric drawing the vertical direction is radius and the lower edge is the axis, not a wall.
Area scales with radius squared: a 15 mm lance radius opening into a 104.5 mm reactor radius is an area ratio of about 49.
A sudden expansion creates a recirculation zone whose length is several step heights, typically about six to eight for turbulent flow behind a step.
Compare variants only if everything except the studied dimension is identical.

understand.title: Why draw only half the plane
understand.text: If the flow is the same at every angle around the axis, the full 3D problem collapses to a 2D one in x and r. The cell volume is 2 pi r dx dr, so the solver still conserves mass in 3D. That is why the lower edge is an axis, not a wall, and why this drawing can be solved in minutes where the 3D bend and honeycomb cannot.

understand.title: Why variants differ by one dimension
understand.text: The 15 mm and 25 mm drawings share 163 mm, 332 mm and the 104.5 mm total reactor height. Only the lance section changes. That is a controlled comparison: any difference in where the coal starts to devolatilise can be attributed to the lance.

understand.title: What the 3D drawing adds and costs
understand.text: The 3D version brings the bend and the honeycomb, which the 2D axisymmetric one cannot represent. It also brings about 127 small channels (see the derivation), which is the reason the mesh in the next figure group is hard to make.

steps.title: From a revolved profile to a volume
steps.note: Revolving the 2D outline about the axis gives the 3D shape. For a constant radius R this is pi R^2 L. The Studio's revolve scene draws the same construction.

steps.title: Area ratio at the step
steps.note: Areas grow with the square of the radius. Using the printed reactor height as the outer radius and the printed lance-section sizes as radii (an assumption: the drawing does not say radius or diameter), the expansion is about 49 times for the base case and 17 times for the 25 mm variant. Checked numerically.

steps.title: Velocity drops by the same factor
steps.note: Continuity for an incompressible stream. Heating changes the density, so this is only the cold-flow picture, but it shows why a narrow jet slows sharply in the reactor.

steps.title: Pressure rise at a sudden expansion
steps.note: Momentum balance across the step with the wall pressure on the step face taken equal to p_1, the standard Borda-Carnot result. It is the reason the energy balance of an expansion loses head even though the flow slows down.

steps.title: Where the flow reattaches
steps.note: For turbulent flow behind a backward-facing step the recirculation reattaches roughly six to eight step heights downstream; the value depends on Reynolds number and inlet profile. With h = 79.5 mm that is about 0.5 m, longer than the 332 mm reactor: the drawn reactor is only about four step heights long. This is an order-of-magnitude estimate, not a result of the study.

steps.title: How many cells in the honeycomb
steps.note: The honeycomb occupies the annulus between the 10 mm inner and 60 mm outer diameters. A regular hexagon whose width across flats is w has area (sqrt 3 / 2) w^2. Taking the printed 5 mm cell size as w and ignoring the 0.25 mm walls gives about 127 channels. Computed from the printed dimensions.

steps.title: Open area of the honeycomb
steps.note: With a wall of thickness t = 0.25 mm between cells (taking the printed spacing as the wall), about 91 percent of the area is open. The estimate assumes thin straight walls and ignores the corners.

worked.title: Area ratio and speed ratio for the 25 mm variant
worked.problem: The 25 mm variant has an inlet-section height of 25 mm and a reactor height of 104.5 mm (from 79.5 + 25). If the cold air leaves the inlet section at 10 m/s, how fast is it, on average, after the step?

solution.text: Take both heights as radii measured from the axis and form the area ratio.
Continuity gives the mean speed after the step.

worked.answer: About 0.6 m/s on average for cold, incompressible flow (the 10 m/s is an illustrative input, not a case value). Heating would raise the speed again through the density drop.

analyze.q: The key lists an air inlet and a coal inlet but no outlet. Which edge would the solver treat as the outlet, and what could go wrong if it were set as a wall?
analyze.hint: Think of mass conservation in a closed domain.

analyze.q: The reactor is about four step heights long, but a turbulent recirculation needs six to eight to reattach. What does that imply for the flow at the right-hand boundary of the domain?
analyze.hint: Where do you want the outlet boundary to sit relative to the recirculation?

analyze.q: In the co-injection drawing the hydrogen inlet lies between two lance walls. How does this change the number of boundary-condition entries compared with the base case?
analyze.hint: Count the numbered tags in the two drawings.

evaluate.q: The drawings mix labels such as 15 mm and 25 mm without saying radius or diameter. How much does that ambiguity matter for the area-ratio estimate?
evaluate.hint: Area scales with the square, so a factor of two in size is a factor of four in area.

evaluate.q: A 2D axisymmetric model replaces a rig that has a bend and a honeycomb. Which results from it would you trust, and which would you not?
evaluate.hint: Think of anything that depends on swirl, the bend or the honeycomb.

create: Redraw the base-case drawing with the outlet, the axis of symmetry and the flow direction labelled, radii marked with R, and the step height printed.
Design a second variant that changes only the reactor length so that it spans eight step heights, and say which printed dimension you would change and what the cost is.

checks.q: In an axisymmetric drawing, what is the horizontal line at the bottom of the domain?
checks.answer: The axis of symmetry, not a wall. The vertical direction is radius and the solver treats the lower edge as the centreline.

checks.q: A section of 15 mm radius opens into a 104.5 mm radius reactor. By what factor does the flow area grow?
checks.hint: Use the square of the ratio.
checks.answer: (104.5/15)^2, about 48.5, so mean speed of a cold incompressible stream drops by that factor.

checks.q: The 25 mm variant has a 79.5 mm step and a 332 mm reactor. Is the reactor long enough for the recirculation to reattach?
checks.hint: Compare 332 with six to eight step heights.
checks.answer: 332 / 79.5 is about 4.2 step heights, shorter than the usual six to eight, so the recirculation will probably reach the outlet area: the outlet boundary condition then matters more.

checks.q: The study compares 15 mm and 25 mm lances. What must be identical for the comparison to be fair?
checks.answer: Reactor size, inlet flows and temperatures, coal feed rate and particle properties, mesh strategy and models. Only the lance section may change.

checks.q: How would you add a hydrogen inlet to the base-case drawing without changing the reactor?
checks.answer: Split the lance section with another wall to form a separate annular inlet, label it, and give it its own flow rate and composition, leaving the 163 mm, 332 mm and reactor height untouched.
